title: The six-tusked elephant
hook: an elephant helps the hunter who wounded him cut his tusks (Jataka 514)

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Sivi's dana, his giving, gave both his eyes to a blind stranger. Your line was what he gave. Did you give the thing that cost you? Today, a gift given to an enemy. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

The arrow comes from below. An elephant king walks a forest path, and a hunter hidden in a pit shoots a poisoned arrow up into him. In the Jataka this elephant is Chaddanta, the six-tusked, the leader of a great herd. The story could end with him crushing the man in the pit. Every part of him has the strength to do it. It doesn't end that way. Today, what the wounded elephant does instead.
screen: `AN ARROW FROM BELOW.` → `A HUNTER IN A PIT.` → `THE STRENGTH TO CRUSH HIM.`

segments.voice: First, how it started. Chaddanta had two wives, and one of them, Culla-subhadda, came to believe he favored the other. The slight was small, the story makes clear: a shower of blossoms that fell on the wrong wife. She nursed it until she died wishing for revenge, and she was reborn as a queen in a human kingdom. Second, the hunter. As queen, she sent a hunter named Sonuttara to find the elephant and bring back his tusks. He made the long journey and hid in a pit, wearing the yellow robe of a renunciant. Third, the turn. Wounded, Chaddanta went for him, then saw the robe and stopped. He would not harm someone wearing that cloth, even someone wearing it as a trick. He asked the hunter why, and heard about the queen, and understood who wanted him dead. Then the hunter tried to saw off the tusks and couldn't manage it. So Chaddanta took the saw in his own trunk, cut the tusks himself, handed them over, and died. Fourth, what the tale doesn't say. It doesn't say the wound didn't matter. It doesn't call the hunter good. It shows someone who had every right to strike back, and chose to help instead. When the queen saw the tusks, the story says, she remembered who he had been, and grief overwhelmed her. The grudge ran the whole story. The elephant is the one who stopped it.
screen: `A GRUDGE OVER FALLING BLOSSOMS.` · `A HUNTER IN A YELLOW ROBE.` · `HE STOPS, AND ASKS WHY.` · `THE SAW IN HIS OWN TRUNK.` · then, large: `HE HELPED THE HUNTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: loosen one hurt. Sit and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind a small injury, not the biggest one you carry. A sharp word. A slight at work. Someone who took the credit. See if you can find where it sits in the body, the jaw, the chest, the stomach. You don't have to excuse it or call it fine. Just try, for one breath, setting it down, the way the elephant stopped at the sight of a robe. If it comes back, notice that too, and set it down again. The bell holds the time.
Chaddanta. The six-tusked elephant king who, wounded by a hunter, helped him take the tusks he came for. Today's word.
Your line: he helped the hunter. When the small hurt you chose comes back today, answer it with one helpful act instead of a sharp one. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers retell the Chaddanta story as a tale of patience and forgiveness; Buddhists practice letting go of resentment through reflection and loving-kindness meditation.

fork.setup: you're Chaddanta, wounded by a hunter in a pit. you see he's wearing a renunciant's robe. what do you do?
options: crush him anyway; he shot you.
stop, and ask him why he did it.
turn away into the forest and leave him.
fork.reveal: he stops at the sight of the robe and asks why; when the hunter can't cut the tusks, the elephant cuts them for him.

original.note: Pali Chaddanta, the elephant's name, given in English as six-tusked.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about a noble animal.
what it means: forgiveness under the worst pressure; the wounded elephant helps the man who shot him.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 514 follows a grudge from one life into the next, and the elephant stops it; some readers stress that he honors the robe itself, whoever wears it.

notes: Confirm: Culla-subhadda's slight (blossoms from a shaken sal tree falling on Maha-subhadda); her death wishing revenge and rebirth as queen Subhadda of Benares; the hunter Sonuttara in a yellow robe hiding in a pit; the elephant sawing his own tusks; the queen's grief on seeing them (the text has her die of grief; script says 'grief overwhelmed her').
The name Chaddanta is glossed only as 'given in English as six-tusked'; commentary explains six-colored rays from the tusks. No etymology claimed.
